questions.prompt: Volcanoes and earthquakes often line up along the same belts on a world map, such as the ring around the Pacific Ocean. Why do many of them occur in related regions?
questions.accessiblePrompt: On a world map, volcanoes and earthquakes often line up along the same belts, such as the ring around the edge of the Pacific Ocean. Why do many of them occur in related regions?

choices.text: Both are linked to tectonic plates interacting, with some exceptions far from plate edges.
choices.rationale: Correct: plate interactions both make magma and build stress, so the two hazards share belts; hot spots and faults inside plates are the exceptions.

choices.text: Most earthquakes are set off by erupting volcanoes, so the shaking clusters around them.
choices.rationale: Most strong earthquakes come from plates or faults slipping, not from eruptions; the San Andreas transform boundary shakes with no volcanoes nearby.

choices.text: Those belts lie close to the equator, where sunshine heats the rock enough to melt it.
choices.rationale: The Pacific belt reaches far from the equator, up to Alaska, and the sun's warmth reaches only the top of the ground, not the deep rock that melts.

choices.text: Strong shaking cracks the ground open, and each crack soon grows into a new volcano.
choices.rationale: Shaking does not create magma. Magma forms only where added material, lower pressure or a rising plume lets rock melt.

questions.explanation: Where plates collide, spread apart or grind past each other, rock can melt into magma and stress can build until rock slips. That is why both hazards trace many of the same belts, such as the Pacific Ring of Fire. The pattern has exceptions: hot spots like Hawaii and faults inside plates, like the New Madrid zone, are active far from any boundary.
questions.misconception: Volcanoes and earthquakes are found together because one always causes the other.
questions.hint: Which choice gives one cause that could both melt rock and build up stress in it?

questions.explanation: Rock can melt in more than one way. Adding water lowers the temperature at which rock melts, and lowering the pressure lets already-hot rock melt without extra heating. At a hot spot, rock hotter than its surroundings rises, and it also melts partly because the pressure on it drops as it rises. Friction between moving plates is not what makes this magma; at a subduction zone, water from the sinking plate does the main work.

questions.hint: One reason adds material, one comes from plates moving apart, and one needs rock that is hotter than its surroundings.

questions.prompt: Why does thick, sticky magma tend to cause explosive eruptions?
questions.accessiblePrompt: Why does thick, sticky magma tend to cause explosive eruptions?

choices.rationale: Correct: trapped gas pressure, not speed or heat, drives the explosion.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in order to show how stress along a plate boundary turns into an earthquake.
questions.accessiblePrompt: Put these steps in order to show how stress along a plate boundary turns into an earthquake. The steps are: the rock suddenly slips, and the stored energy spreads out as seismic waves; the plates keep moving, but their rough edges catch and lock; the edges lock again, and stress begins to build once more; stress builds in the rock along the stuck boundary; the stress grows greater than the locked edges can hold.

items.text: The rock suddenly slips, and the stored energy spreads out as seismic waves
items.rationale: Slip happens only after the stress has grown too great; the waves are its result.

items.text: The plates keep moving, but their rough edges catch and lock
items.rationale: Locking comes first: without stuck edges, no stress could build.

items.text: The edges lock again, and stress begins to build once more
items.rationale: After the slip, the edges catch again, restarting the cycle, so this is last.

items.text: Stress builds in the rock along the stuck boundary
items.rationale: While the edges are locked and the plates keep moving, stress accumulates.

items.text: The stress grows greater than the locked edges can hold
